title: 7 days split program review (Rubgy focus)
summary: NH reviews a rugby player's squat-every-day home program, explaining that daily squatting sacrifices volume for frequency and intensity and suits strength better than size. He tweaks rep schemes (evolving overhead press sets, more biceps volume), then lays out how to convert it into a pull-push-legs split with heavy and light days, using fartlek running and sprints on light days for rugby conditioning.
claims: When submitting a program, mention outside sports; otherwise he assumes lifting is all you do and judges tonnage and recovery accordingly
Volume, frequency and intensity cannot all be maxed on one movement pattern at once; for naturals something will break
Squatting every day sacrifices volume: you work up to around 90% with little work, so daily tonnage is low but weekly tonnage is high, and you get very neurologically efficient
For pure hypertrophy, widowmaker squats beat squatting every day
Squatting every day is the best way to gain squat strength, while a widowmaker squat about once every four days is best for size
Regulating daily squats from a minimum up to a max based on feel is a good way to manage intensity
3x5 overhead press is low volume for a rugby player; do 6 sets: 3x5 for stable volume plus 3x2-5 evolving to push intensity
Take pull-ups and calisthenics to failure because your return to baseline on them is high
Rather than a fixed 3x5 then 2x10, use 3x2-5 then 2x10 back-offs so you get both intensity and pump volume
For bench hypertrophy he gets better gains staying lower in intensity and higher in volume; the bench is the most skill-dependent big lift and a misgrooved rep can't be ground out
Prioritize vertical pulls; they decompress the spine, valuable for a rugby player compressed in scrums
2x10 barbell curls do nothing; do 4x8-12 if you want bigger biceps, or skip them
Supersetting pull-ups with barbell curls isn't synergistic but won't hurt performance
RDLs at 5x10 are fine because hamstrings reproduce muscular endurance well and you go full range; 5x10 on bench would be sandbagging
High-rep band face pulls keep the rotator cuff healthy and build the upper back
Overhead pressing twice a week won't fry the shoulders if you press on top of you, not in front
Do inverted rows with supinated, pronated and neutral grips
With lower back out of the equation he can do upper back pulls day in, day out
Biceps recover within three days, so four sets is fine
Getting winded from daily squats means you need more cardio; sprinters train by repeating sprints
Squatting every day still needs occasional all-out max days to force adaptation
The viewer added 50 lb to his squat with squat every day
Sprinting and cardio depend on posture; a tired lower body collapses posture and limits cardiovascular work
Include some pull from the floor; it need not be conventional, trap bar or Jefferson are fine
Heavy/medium/light days are a simplistic way to manipulate volume and intensity
He dislikes push-pull-legs ordering because deadlifts on pull day leave you tired for legs, and squats are harder to recover from and more prone to postural fatigue; pull-push-legs-rest is better
For rugby, fartlek-style 'Indian runs' (jog a minute, sprint five seconds, repeat) match the sport's demands
Place sprints and longer cardio on days off or after leg day before a push day, and use light days for cardio since they won't hurt performance
